planting.note: Tuck small rooted offsets into gritty soil or wall crevices in spring so they establish before summer heat.

directions: This tiny Mediterranean species forms dense mats of round, blue-gray beads no bigger than a grain of rice, packed tightly along creeping stems. Small white to pale pink starry flowers appear on short stalks in early summer, but the main appeal is the constant color and texture of the foliage. It thrives in shallow, gritty soil with sharp drainage, making it a natural for stone walls, gravel troughs, and roof gardens where richer soil would cause rot. Winter wet is the main hazard, so raised or sloped plantings suit it far better than flat, heavy beds.

planting.note: Divide and replant offsets in spring into sharply drained soil so roots knit in before hot weather.

directions: This selection is a noticeably larger-leaved, more vigorous version of the species, with plumper blue-gray beads and a faster spreading habit that fills gaps between paving stones or troughs more quickly. Loose sprays of small white flowers appear in early summer above the foliage mounds. Because the leaves are larger than the type, it holds up a bit better to light foot traffic and dry spells, though it still needs gritty, fast-draining soil to avoid rot. Shear back leggy stems after flowering to keep the mat compact and encourage fresh new growth.

planting.note: Press rooted sprigs into lean soil in spring; established mats spread quickly and rarely need replanting.

directions: This selection of white stonecrop carries small, cylindrical leaves that flush deep bronze-red in full sun and cool weather, turning greener again in shade or during humid summer stretches. Flat clusters of tiny white flowers cover the mat in early summer, drawing bees and other small pollinators. It spreads by rooting along creeping stems, making it useful for filling cracks in pavement or covering a hot, dry slope where little else will grow. Give it poor, well-drained soil and avoid rich beds or heavy mulch, both of which encourage rot and weaken the foliage color.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a container or rock-wall pocket where the variegated foliage can be seen up close.

directions: This variegated sport of October daphne carries rounded, blue-gray leaves in whorls of three, each marked with a creamy yellow blotch in the center that shifts to soft pink tones as nights cool in autumn. Clusters of small star-shaped pink flowers open at the arching stem tips in early to mid fall, coinciding with the best of the fall leaf color. A little midday shade helps preserve the variegation and prevents scorch better than the all-green species tolerates, though it still needs lean, sharply drained soil to perform well. Divide congested clumps in spring, discarding any all-green reverted shoots to keep the variegation strong.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
